comets_intro: A census of CO₂ released by comets, measured in SPHEREx frames. Each point is one comet at the epoch of its census, with the 16–84% range of the production rate Q.

comets_honesty_census: This is a census by pass, not a real-time monitor: SPHEREx revisits each comet only a few times a year, and public data lag by weeks.
comets_honesty_velocity: Q is proportional to the outflow speed. Assuming a speed of 0.50 instead of 0.85 r_h^−0.5 km/s lowers every Q by about {percent}%: treat this as a systematic on top of the plotted range.
comets_honesty_far: Beyond {au} au the band flux is too small for a trustworthy Q. Those points are marked and should not be interpreted.
comets_honesty_systematics: “With systematics” means a band is present (S/N ≥ 5) but the band model fits poorly (χ²ᵣ ≥ 50): the Q shown is not trusted at its quoted precision.

method_intro: How every number on this site is made, checked and limited. Values on this page are read from the same data files the product uses.
method_s1_p1: SPHEREx level-2 images from the DR1 and QR3 releases ({l2}), read straight from the public S3 bucket of NASA/IRSA. The exposure index has {rows} exposures for detectors D4–D6 and {keys} S3 keys; D1–D3 see the same sky as their pair D4–D6, shifted by the dichroic.
method_s1_p2: Nothing is simulated: every image, spectrum and measurement comes from these files, from Gaia DR3 and SIMBAD for positions, or from JPL Horizons for ephemerides.
method_s2_p1: Six H2RG detectors with {pixel}″ pixels share a linear variable filter: each row of a detector sees a slightly different wavelength, so one exposure samples a narrow band per row, and the {n} channels together cover {lo}–{hi} µm. Each exposure lasts {exposure} s.
method_s3_p1: Each pixel's wavelength comes from the full-resolution spectral WCS ({swcs}), never subsampled: subsampling by 4 pixels leaves the 99th percentile within 1 nm but hides jumps of hundreds of nanometres at detector edges. Pixels closer than {edge} px to an edge are excluded from spectra.
method_s3_p2: The v5 calibration moves D5 and D6 by +{shift} nm with respect to the previous one, and leaves D1–D4 unchanged. Independently, our comet census had measured that the CO₂ band of D5 fell about 3.7 ± 0.9 nm short of its laboratory wavelength: the new calibration corrects it in the same direction. We use v5 as published and keep the band shift free in every band fit.
method_s4: 4. Diff λ: the same sky at the same color
method_s4_p1: Because every row sees another wavelength, subtracting two visits leaves a residue on almost every star. Diff λ instead builds, for each frame, a reference of the static sky at that frame's wavelength: it takes up to {k} frames from other visits whose wavelength is within {bw} channel widths, and, per pixel, fits a line in wavelength (3σ clipped) when the references surround the frame's wavelength, or takes their median when they do not (no extrapolation). A frame needs at least {min} references, otherwise Diff λ is reported unavailable.
method_s4_p2: The difference is frame minus reference. What did not change cancels; what moved appears positive where it is and negative where it was; σ is {mad} × the median absolute deviation and sets the ±5σ color scale.
method_s4_p3: Measured in the research notes (not re-run here): χ²ᵣ of comet band fits fell from 104 to 6.5 for 24P and from 440 to 32 for C/2024 J3 when the sky was subtracted this way.
method_s4_alt_raw: Raw subtraction of two Barnard's Star frames at different wavelengths
method_s4_alt_diff: Diff λ of the same frame
method_s4_cap: Barnard's Star, D{det}: raw subtraction (left) and Diff λ (right), same ±5σ scale.
method_s5_p1: Spectra come from a forced fit of the exposure's sampled effective PSF (radius {r} px, free background), with the official quality mask. The mask rejects {flags}. Saturated (OVERFLOW) pixels are not masked, as the SPHEREx team recommends; they are flagged instead.
method_s5_p2: No aperture correction is applied: SPHEREx's absolute gain was calibrated with ePSF photometry, so the sampled ePSF flux already is the calibrated flux. An early version that applied one counted the PSF wings twice and put W2 10% high. The error of each point is σ² plus a {floor}% systematic of the flux, in quadrature.
method_s5_p3: Check against 2MASS and WISE: {n} isolated stars in the fields {fields}. SPHEREx flux divided by catalogue flux, with the scatter between stars:
method_s5_p4: The mean of the five bands is {mean}, and every band lies between {min} and {max}. We quote the whole range, about ±3%, not a single number: an earlier −3.5% in one field did not repeat in the other two.
method_s6_p1: Gas in comets is measured in sky-subtracted spectra with a physical model of the CO₂ ν₃ band (P and R branches, even rotational levels, rotational temperature and a free wavelength shift). CO and H₂O use their own windows: CO in D6 at {co_lo}–{co_hi} µm, H₂O in D4 at {h2o_lo}–{h2o_hi} µm, CO₂ in D5 at {co2_lo}–{co2_hi} µm.
method_s6_p2: The production rate Q comes from a Haser parent model in an aperture of {ap} px with a background ring of {ring_lo}–{ring_hi} px. In the regime of these data Q is nearly proportional to the outflow speed and barely depends on the lifetime, so speed dominates the systematic: assuming {low} instead of {speed} r_h^−0.5 km/s lowers Q by about 40%.
method_s6_p3: Uncertainty: a Monte Carlo of {draws} draws over flux (statistical and profile spread), {cal}% calibration, {g}% g-factor, lognormal lifetime ({tau}) and lognormal speed ({v}); we report the 16, 50 and 84 percentiles.
method_s6_p4: Detection requires S/N ≥ 5 and χ²ᵣ < 50. A comet with a band but a poor fit is shown as “with systematics”; one with 3 ≤ S/N < 5 as “marginal”. The current statuses are {detected} detected, {systematics} with systematics, {marginal} marginal and {none} not detected among {n} comets.
method_s7_p1: Photometry is checked against 2MASS and WISE (section 5). Comet results are compared with published values on the atlas page; a value inside the published range is consistent with it, not an independent confirmation.
method_s7_p2: Asteroid sizes use the NEATM thermal model with η = {eta} ± {sigma}. Against NEOWISE in {cv_n} near-Earth objects the out-of-sample ratio SPHEREx/NEOWISE spans {p16}–{p84} (16–84%), about −{lo}%/+{hi}%. The median of {median} is 1 by construction, because η is fitted to make it so: it is not an accuracy. Every published diameter carries its interval, its evidence tier and a {floor}% systematic floor.
method_s7_p3: Only {avail} of the {total} validation pairs retain their absolute NEOWISE diameter; the page states it and does not fill in the rest.
method_s8_p1: On null spectra (apertures placed where no comet is) the detection rule gave 0 false positives out of 79. This figure comes from the research notes and was not re-run for this build.
method_s8_p2: Pending: a published injection–recovery test of the comet pipeline. Until it exists, no completeness or false-alarm rate is claimed.
method_s9_l1: It is a census by pass, not real time: each object is revisited a few times a year and public data lag by weeks.
method_s9_l2: Gas needs nearby or very productive objects: the band flux scales as Q r_h⁻² Δ⁻². Beyond about 10 au the Q is not trusted.
method_s9_l3: The wavelength of D5 and D6 depends on the spectral calibration version; the shift stays free in every fit.
method_s9_l4: A professional multi-comet catalogue exists (spherex-comet by bumhooLIM, 68 comets, results not public). We do not claim a first census; our contribution is a public, reproducible tool with its checks.
method_s9_l5: Cold-cache stacks take about 5–6 s; the precomputed targets load instantly.
method_s10_p1: The record below is generated from the product's own files at commit {commit}. Source code, pipelines and tests are in the repository.

about_intro: Breathing Comets is a public tool to see how the infrared sky changes, built with real SPHEREx images, for NASA Space Apps 2026.
about_s1_p1: SPHEREx maps the whole sky in {n} colors of infrared light, every six months. Breathing Comets turns that archive into a time machine: type any coordinates and watch the same patch of sky across dates, see what moved, read a spectrum from any pixel, and follow the gas that comets release.
about_s1_p2: Everything shown is a real SPHEREx frame or a measurement made from one, with its uncertainty and its caveats. Where something is not available or not verified, the page says so instead of filling the gap.
about_s2_p1: Planet X and SPHEREx, an advanced challenge of the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The brief asks for a public web tool that displays SPHEREx images and makes it easy for anyone to see how they change over time. Pluto was found by comparing two images of the same sky; the same idea, applied to infrared images, is the starting point here.
about_l_sky: Open the sky: Barnard's Star, with its real frames and the Gaia prediction of its motion
about_l_comets: Comet atlas: CO₂ released by {n} comets, with status, uncertainty and caveats
about_l_neo: Small-Body Lab: asteroid sizes with intervals and evidence tiers
about_l_method: Method: how every number is made, checked and limited
about_s4_intro: This project is independent. It is not a NASA product and uses no NASA logos. All data are public and belong to their providers.
about_u_gaia: Star positions, proper motions and parallaxes
about_u_wise: Photometry checks and asteroid size validation
about_d_jpl: Horizons, Small-Body Database and SB Identification
about_u_jpl: Ephemerides and identification of moving objects
about_u_simbad: Name resolution and star catalogue positions
about_u_aladin: Sky viewer in Lab mode (Boch & Fernique 2014; Baumann et al. 2022)
about_u_astropy: Coordinates, WCS and image reprojection (Astropy Collaboration 2022)
about_s5_p1: We used Claude Code (Anthropic) as an assistant for research, code and writing. Its results were checked against independent data, such as 2MASS and WISE photometry, published comet values and NEOWISE sizes, and an audit corrected several figures before publication. The checks and what remains unverified are listed in the method page.
about_s5_p2: No image on this site is generated by AI: every picture is a real SPHEREx frame or a plot of measured data.
about_s6_p1: Geist and Geist Mono are distributed under the SIL Open Font License 1.1. Aladin Lite is distributed under GPL-3. The source code of this site is public on GitHub.
tour_nudge_body: Take a 30-second tour of how to read a SPHEREx plate.
tour_s1_body: Type a star, a comet or coordinates, or pick one of the five prepared targets underneath.
tour_s2_body: Epoch shows a single frame. Blink flips between two dates so anything that moved jumps out. Diff λ subtracts what the neighbouring colors predict, so only real change stays.
tour_s3_body: Every pixel is measured data. Scroll to zoom, drag to pan and click a pixel to read its spectrum. The blue cross is the position Gaia predicts for the star.
tour_s4_body: Press Play or step through the frames. Each frame is one SPHEREx color on one date, and the ruler shows when they were taken.
tour_s5_body: Measured values with their uncertainty and caveats, plus shortcuts that set up a comparison for you.
tour_s6_body: Story is the guided view; Lab, on wider screens, adds sky layers and an inspector. Share copies a link that restores exactly this view.
